earlier_scan.source_named: Okell, John (1995), 'Three Burmese Dialects' (Papers in Southeast Asian Linguistics 13) — descriptive coverage of Intha

new_statements.quote: [p. 58, §3.2.1.1 TONES] high plain /á/ high creaky /a̰/ low /a/ high stop /aʔ/ weak /ə/ ... [§3.2.2] Tones are on the whole similar to SB tones, but there are differences between the intonation patterns of IT and those of SB, which are of course matched by differences in the realisation of syllable tone, especially at the end of a sentence, and sometimes at the end of a clause. The difference is so marked in the case of a small number of sentence-final and clause-final particles (curiously, not all are so affected), that it proved impossible to assign any of the usual phonemic tones to them. [p. 69, §3.3.2.2 WEAKENING] Weakening occurs in IT much as in SB, though there are indications that it is less used.
new_statements.citation: Okell, John. 1995. Three Burmese dialects. In David Bradley (ed.), Papers in Southeast Asian Linguistics No. 13: Studies in Burmese languages, 1-138. Pacific Linguistics A-83. Canberra: Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-A83.1
new_statements.locator: §3.2.1.1 Tones and §3.2.2 Phoneme description, p. 58; §3.3.2.2 Weakening, p. 69
new_statements.rule_in_words: Intha is described as a tone language with the Standard Burmese system (three tones on open/nasal syllables, a stopped syllable type, and a 'weak' toneless schwa syllable); the only prominence-related phenomenon described is 'weakening', i.e. reduction of non-final syllables to /ə/ as in Standard Burmese, said to be somewhat less used in Intha. No word-stress placement rule is stated anywhere in the Intha section; the word 'stress' does not occur in Okell's paper.
new_statements.exceptions: Some sentence-final and clause-final particles (/wa (wo), ma (mo), sho, lo, le/) cannot be assigned a phonemic tone and are marked with a macron; in some words the weak syllable is dropped entirely or fused (p. 69).
new_statements.domain_note: Syllable tone described at word and sentence level from recorded narratives (Ywa-ma village, west bank of Inle Lake, 1961 and 1969); weakening concerns non-final syllables of polysyllabic words. Tone symbols in the quote were rendered from the PDF's diacritics (acute = high plain/creaky per the volume's conventions; the text layer garbles them as 1+1).
new_statements.identity_note: Okell 1995 describes Intha (IT) of Ywa-ma and neighbouring west-bank villages of Inle Lake (Nyaungshwe), recorded 1961 and 1969; Danu (the other half of Glottolog's inth1238) is not described there (Bradley's preface calls Danu and Taungyo 'virtually undescribed'). The Khin Sandar Toe 2018 article concerns Danu of the Nawnghkio area (vocabulary only). Naksuk 2012/2014 describe Intha of Inle Lake, Nyaung Shwe Township.

sources.locator: §3.2.1.1 Tones and §3.2.2 Phoneme description, p. 58; §3.3.2.2 Weakening, p. 69
sources.note: No use of the word 'stress' for Intha. Tone inventory (p. 58): high plain, high creaky, low, high stop, weak /ə/. 'Tones are on the whole similar to SB tones' with intonation differences at sentence/clause end; some final particles cannot be assigned a phonemic tone (p. 58). 'Weakening occurs in IT much as in SB, though there are indications that it is less used' (p. 69), i.e. reduced schwa syllables in non-final position as in Standard Burmese. No word-stress rule stated.

sources.citation: Bradley, David. 1995. Preface / Transcription conventions. In Bradley (ed.), Papers in Southeast Asian Linguistics No. 13, v-xii. Pacific Linguistics A-83.
sources.note: For Standard Burmese (not Intha specifically): three tones plus stopped syllables; 'non-final syllables in a two or more syllable word have an additional alternative, called weak or reduced, which consists of an initial consonant plus the vowel /ə/... a neutralisation of vowel and tonal contrasts' (p. x). No stress statement.
